title: ‘His wife was horrified’: did Edward Hopper paint his sexual problems?
text:
It should have been a happy occasion. In 1950, an Edward Hopper retrospective was staged at the Whitney Museum of American Art in New York – but the artist’s wife, the painter Josephine (Jo) Nivison Hopper, was in a fury. The show’s catalogue, written by the museum’s director, had originally stated that in 1924 Edward “married the artist Josephine Nivison Hopper”, yet in the final version, the phrase “the artist” had been removed. “I’m not allowed to exist even in my husband’s biography,” Jo seethed in a private notebook that has just come to light. “And that’s all right with EH.”
Due to her own strenuous efforts, Jo not only exists, but is a vital protagonist in my new biography of Edward Hopper. Jo once contemplated writing her husband’s biography herself, having amassed such an overwhelming body of material documenting their tumultuous marriage. As Edward’s creative partner, muse, curator, producer and unofficial manager, Jo produced 35 years’ worth of daily diaries, almost 100 notebooks, reels of letters, and four ledger books documenting Edward’s works.
A self-confessed “pack-rat”, she preserved everything from their film and theatre ticket stubs to magazines, catalogues and photographs. This vast material legacy, much of it housed at the Whitney, would form the backbone of my biography, the first on Edward in 30 years and only the second ever.
I was able to draw on many unpublished notebooks and diaries (including Edward’s sole notebook on art), which reveal new and poignant details about the Hoppers’ complex relationship and artistic rivalry. In one firecracker of a notebook spanning nearly 80 pages, Jo not only reveals the alarming abuse she suffered and their unsatisfactory sex life, but also recounts the whirlwind farce of their wedding day that resulted in a mad rush from church to church after Edward, who was not baptised, was turned away by a reverend. They lost their best man along the way.
Jo ultimately decided against writing Edward’s biography, explaining: “To have to think and weigh and be explicit – this big, tall, lonely, silent man … it would need expert reporting and memory to repeat his exact words for any fairness.” Indeed, Edward gave so little away that he still presents as an enigma. This is the Edward we both see and feel in such iconic works as his haunting Nighthawks, showing four people in a diner; his disquieting Automat, in which a lone woman sits in a cafe; and his ode to modern melancholia, Hotel Room, featuring another solitary woman poised on the edge of a bed reading.
However, I decided to begin with the artist’s lesser-known works and little explored formative years. I did not expect to discover that all of Edward’s earliest oils – long claimed to be originals, some supposedly depicting his home town of Nyack in upstate New York – were in fact copies from colour reproductions of other artists’ works found in Victorian periodicals, replete with copying instructions. Of course, all aspiring artists copy, but this discovery upended the myth that Edward’s painting talent arose in an art historical vacuum, showing him engaging with the American art of his era from an early age.
It is still little-recognised that the majority of Edward’s paintings are of regional subjects, mostly in New England, rather than the cityscapes he is best known for. And of all his subjects, it was a lighthouse in the remote Maine village of Two Lights that he painted the most. I wanted to know why.
The Hoppers drove to Two Lights in the summer of 1927. “We fell in love with the lighthouse,” Jo wrote, but when she attempted “a harmless little watercolour”, Edward huffed, saying: “If you’re going to paint it – I won’t.” Jo was left to sulk on the rocks, where she wrote a list of “blessings of attributes of E to be remembered in times of stress”. Sadly, that list did little to redeem Jo’s often damning opinion of her husband, whom she called a “sadist” and a “prize hog”.
Jo makes clear that Edward’s possessiveness derived from a profound identification with the lighthouse. At 6ft 4in tall, he repeatedly inferred that the awkward, tall architectures in his paintings were anthropomorphic self-portraits. In 1946, Jo wrote: “Those lighthouses are self-portraits.” She added: “That ego is impenetrable … It was pitiful to see all the poor dead birds that had run into [the lighthouses] on a dark night. I know just how they felt. That bright light on the top had deceived them.”
But for Edward, works such as 1929’s The Lighthouse at Two Lights was as close to celebratory as his art ever came. Cherishing the literature of such esteemed writers as Walt Whitman and Ralph Waldo Emerson, who embodied a historic tradition of heroic American solitude, Edward envisaged the lighthouse as a beacon of American individualism, the philosophy that he most ardently observed.
The political ramifications of his lighthouse did not stop there. In seeking to paint and thereby aggrandise New England’s regional icons, Edward, among others, sated the appetite of a fiercely nationalist and isolationist press that hungered for representations of the regional “American scene”. New England’s white Anglo-Saxon lineage and its colonial beginnings were also crucial aspects of its appeal. Edward’s work would be repeatedly referred to as “Anglo-Saxon” and “Puritan” for decades as a means of stressing his quintessential Americanness. In both his art and letters of the period, Edward capitalised on these currents, even telling one critic: “You did a swell job on me as a Puritan.”
Captain Ed Staples, a fictionalised self-portrait showing the artist as a New England sea captain in 1928, embodies these ideas. Combing through ancestral records, I discovered that the Staples surname belonged to the historic lighthouse family that had co-founded Two Lights, and that the Hopper and Staples families became firm friends. In creating this New England alter ego, Edward surely knew what he was doing. Capt Ed Staples, sadly destroyed in a 1929 train crash, was the “all-American” Edward Hopper incarnate.
As Edward’s fortunes ascended in the late 1920s, Jo’s dwindled. She had previously enjoyed artistic success in modernist circles and, in 1923, it was she who had encouraged Edward to paint in watercolours, which led to a landmark sale and the securing of Edward’s lifetime gallerist. But Edward almost never sought to help Jo with her career, and she never forgave him his neglect, nor his dismissal of female artists in general. To him, she wrote, “they were nil – zero minus etc”. Jo’s diaries consistently document Edward’s denigration of her art as well as instances of domestic abuse – albeit with flashes of lightness and humour – painting a picture of a troubled marriage and a deeply repressed man.
While they never betray the violent altercations that shocked readers when extracts from Jo’s diaries were first published in Gail Levin’s 1995 biography, Edward’s paintings, such as Four Lane Road, make the couple’s tension explicit. The female figure, confined to the interior of a gas station, leans out of the window, her mouth open, breaking the reverie of the man sitting outside, who intriguingly resembles Captain Ed Staples. Jo was horrified to see that Edward was “making the most evil face on the woman at window … a regular shrike, expressive of what he’s feeling about me”. In the painting’s ledger book entry, Jo pointedly remarked: “Woman … finds his serenity a trial.”
Elsewhere, Edward’s 1959 work Excursion into Philosophy suggests the Hoppers’ incompatible sexual relationship. It portrays a woman on a bed, turned away with her naked buttocks on display. This was surely a nod to Edward’s sexual preferences, which Jo referred to as “attacks from the rear”. Beside the woman’s buttocks is an open book that deliberately echoes their shape. Describing the painting, Jo said it was a “book of Plato … resorted to on morning after episode with young woman”. Plato clearly provides little solace for the man, who stares into a rectangle of sunlight, grappling with what seems to be his shame in the harsh light of day.
Jo modelled for Edward’s 1941 painting Girlie Show, featuring a nude burlesque performer. She could not decide whether the woman was an autonomous performer or an object of male desire, variously naming her a “minx”, “vixen” and “siren.” Ultimately, Jo reflected that she was “not as heroic” as the “big strong creature that parades so triumphantly”. On a stray scrap of paper that I found, Jo scathingly documented her experience as a model: “One doesn’t exist at all in any personal sense. He isn’t painting you. He raves about the wall … Little does he care how you freeze … with scarcely a stitch on of a cold night to see how light falls on your shivering flesh.”
Edward’s final oil painting, 1966’s Two Comedians, chose at last to acknowledge Jo as an equal partner. It shows Edward and Jo donning ruffs as a smiling Pierrot and Pierrette on a stage, holding hands and bowing out after a life together – with a nod to their favourite film Les Enfants du Paradis, the swooningly romantic 1945 tribute to theatre. “This marriage has been the one great enterprise – my kingdom come,” Jo wrote in 1939. “Our Kingdom … Of all the profoundest gifts of God: fidelity, wisely or not.”
